topics.title: Peripheral Devices
notes: Peripheral devices are devices connected to a computer system but not part of its core architecture (monitor, mouse, keyboard, printer).
Input devices: keyboard, mouse, scanner, trackball, joystick, touch screen, touchpad, digitizer, bar code reader, MICR, optical mark reader, card reader, paper tape reader.
Output devices: monitor (CRT, LCD, LED, plasma), printers (impact: dot matrix, daisy wheel, drum, chain; non-impact: inkjet, laser), plotter, speaker, headphone, projector.
Storage devices: primary (RAM, ROM, cache) and secondary (hard disk, floppy disk, optical disc CD/DVD/Blu-ray, pen drive, magnetic tape, memory card, flash memory, USB).
Difference between CPU and peripherals: CPU is electronic and fast, works in words and synchronously. Peripherals are electro-mechanical, slower, work in bytes and asynchronously.

Input devices (slides): OCR (optical character recognition), light pen, touchpad, digitizer, barcode reader, MICR (magnetic ink character recognition), OMR (optical mark reader), card reader, paper tape reader.
Monitors: CRT (cathode ray tube) is the older type; non-CRT displays are LCD, LED and plasma (PDP).
Impact printers strike a ribbon: dot matrix, daisy wheel, drum and chain (line) printers. Non-impact printers: inkjet and laser.
Other output devices on the slides: speaker, headphone, plotter, and COM (computer output microfilm).

Storage devices (slides): primary = RAM, ROM, cache. Secondary = magnetic tape, magnetic disk (hard disk, floppy disk FDD), optical disc (CD-ROM, DVD, Blu-ray), flash memory (USB pen drive, memory card, SD card, SSD).

topics.title: Input-Output Interface
notes: The I/O interface gives a method to transfer information between the internal storage (CPU and memory) and external I/O devices, because peripherals need special communication links to connect to the CPU.
Functions of the I/O interface: synchronizes the operating speed of the CPU with the I/O devices; selects the correct I/O device; provides control and timing signals; allows data buffering.
An interface receives four types of commands: control, status, data output and data input.

topics.title: Synchronous & Asynchronous Data Transfer
notes: Synchronous transmission: sender and receiver share a common clock. Data is sent in fixed intervals with timing signals. It is faster and easier to design, but needs clock synchronization.

Asynchronous transmission: no common clock. Each character has start and stop bits and irregular time gaps between characters. It is simpler in hardware, slower than synchronous, and needs control signals (strobe or handshaking). Example: email, forum.

Strobe control: a separate control signal (strobe) tells the receiver when the data is valid. Source-initiated strobe: source sends the strobe after placing data. Destination-initiated strobe: destination sends the strobe when it is ready.
Handshaking: two control lines (data valid / data accepted in source-initiated; ready for data / data valid in destination-initiated) ensure both devices are ready. It is more reliable than strobe.
Terminology: sender (device that transfers data), receiver (device that receives data), packet (discrete unit of data).

Synchronous vs asynchronous (slide table): Synchronous = common clock shared, easy to design, faster, costlier, data sent in frames or blocks. Asynchronous = not based on a predetermined timing pattern, complex, slower, cheaper, data sent as bytes or characters.
Asynchronous transfer needs control signals so that the time at which each device sends data is known. It allows other devices to do processing before the transfer is done.
Asynchronous examples on the slide: email, forum, radio.

Strobe control (slide): bits are transmitted one at a time, without a clock. The strobe signal is generated by the transmitting device and sent before the data (leading strobe) or after the data (trailing strobe).
Classification of asynchronous transfer: Strobe method (source initiated, destination initiated) and Handshaking method (source initiated, destination initiated).

Handshaking guarantees synchronized and dependable data delivery, because both devices are prepared before data is sent. Source-initiated handshake: place data and enable DATA VALID; accept data and enable DATA ACCEPTED; disable DATA VALID; disable DATA ACCEPTED (back to initial state). Destination-initiated handshake: enable READY FOR DATA; place data and enable DATA VALID; accept data and disable READY FOR DATA; disable DATA VALID (initial state).

Terminology (slide): Sender = machine that transfers data. Receiver = device that receives data. Packet = discrete unit of transmitted/received data. Buffer = short-term location for storing incoming or departing data.

topics.title: Modes of Data Transfer
notes: Data transfer between CPU and I/O devices can be done in three ways: Programmed I/O, Interrupt-initiated I/O and Direct Memory Access (DMA).

Programmed I/O: the CPU actively controls the transfer. The CPU repeatedly checks (polls) the status flag of the device; each data item transfer is started by an instruction in the program. The CPU is busy in every transfer (wasteful). The interface loads data into a data register, sets a flag in the status register, and the CPU reads the data when flag = 1.

Interrupt-initiated I/O: overcomes the waste of programmed I/O. When the interface finds the device is ready, it sends an interrupt to the CPU. The CPU stops its task, services the I/O transfer, and returns to its previous task. It is asynchronous and reduces CPU idle time.

DMA (Direct Memory Access): fast devices (like magnetic disks) transfer data directly to or from memory through the memory bus, without CPU intervention. A DMA controller takes control of the bus (HOLD/HLDA handshake). Used for bulk transfers, and it is the most efficient mode for large data.

Modes of data transfer (slide): the three modes are Programmed I/O, Interrupt-initiated I/O and DMA. They aim to improve efficiency by managing the trade-off between CPU involvement and data transfer speed (DMA reduces CPU intervention). They also improve resource utilization and give flexibility: programmed I/O gives precise control, DMA gives high-speed autonomous transfer.

Programmed I/O (slide): the I/O device cannot access memory directly, so it needs an instruction in the CPU program. Each data item transfer is started by an instruction. Transfer is usually between a CPU register and memory. It needs constant monitoring of the device by the CPU, which keeps the processor busy and degrades system performance.

Programmed I/O interface (slide diagram): CPU lines are data bus, address bus, I/O read and I/O write. The interface has a data register and a status register containing flag bit F. Device side lines are I/O bus, data valid and data accepted.

Programmed I/O steps: (1) interface accepts the byte into its data register and enables data accepted; (2) interface sets flag F in the status register; (3) if F = 1 the CPU reads the data from the data register; (4) if F = 0 the interface disables data accepted and the device can send the next byte.
Interrupt-initiated I/O characteristics: asynchronous operation; reduces CPU involvement during idle times; efficient for devices with unpredictable or slow response times.

DMA (slide): transfer between fast storage (magnetic disk) and memory is limited by CPU speed, so peripherals communicate with memory over the memory buses without CPU intervention. During DMA the CPU is idle and has no control over the memory buses. The DMA controller takes over the buses.

DMA signals (slide diagram): the DMA controller sends BR (bus request) to the processor's HOLD input. The processor replies on HLDA (hold acknowledge). Then the processor sends BG (bus grant) to the DMA controller, which then controls the bus for the transfer between memory and the I/O device.

topics.title: Memory Hierarchy & Types of Memory
notes: Memory is used to store data and instructions. Three main factors when selecting memory: size, data access speed and cost.

Memory hierarchy arranges memory in levels: cache (fastest, smallest, most expensive), main memory (primary), magnetic disk and magnetic tape (secondary/auxiliary: slowest, cheapest, largest). Speed decreases and capacity increases as we move down the hierarchy.
Primary memory (internal): directly accessible by the CPU, volatile, costly, fast access, lower capacity. Examples: RAM, ROM, cache.
Secondary memory (external/auxiliary): not directly accessible by the CPU, non-volatile, cheap, huge capacity, slower. Examples: magnetic tape, magnetic disk, optical disk, pen drive.

RAM (Random Access Memory): read-write, volatile, main memory, stores the programs and data actively used. Static RAM stores bits in flip-flops (no refresh, faster, used in cache). Dynamic RAM stores bits as charge on a capacitor (needs refreshing, cheaper and denser).

ROM (Read Only Memory): non-volatile, stores permanent programs and data (firmware), read operation only. Types: PROM (programmable once by the user), EPROM (erased by UV light and reprogrammed), EEPROM (erased electrically, one byte at a time, so reprogramming is slow).
Memory selection (slide): three main areas to consider are size of memory, data access speed and cost of memory.

Needs of main memory (slide): all programs, files and data are kept in secondary storage (larger, slower). Secondary memory cannot be accessed directly by the CPU, so the OS loads the process to be executed into primary memory, which the CPU can access directly. This optimizes system performance.

Primary vs secondary (slide table): Primary = internal, directly accessible by CPU, volatile, lower capacity than secondary, costly, fast access, e.g. RAM, ROM, cache. Secondary = external, not directly accessible by CPU, non-volatile, huge storage, cheap, e.g. hard disk (magnetic disk), magnetic tape.

Note: the slide table lists secondary memory as having 'lower access time' in one place, while the same slides say secondary memory is slower than primary. Use the general rule: primary is faster, secondary is slower.

Memory hierarchy (slide): memory has multiple levels with different size and cost. Cache and main memory are faster but smaller and costlier; some memories have higher storage but are slower. Access time is not the same for all memory types. The pyramid from top to bottom is: register, cache memory, main memory (primary), magnetic disk, magnetic tape (auxiliary).

RAM (slide): complete name Random Access Memory; also called computer memory or main memory; short-term data storage that keeps what the computer is actively using; read-write; limited size but high speed; volatile. The more programs running, the more RAM needed.

Classification of RAM (slide): Static RAM stores bits in flip-flops, valid as long as power is supplied, faster, used for cache. Dynamic RAM stores bits as charge on a capacitor, needs refresh circuitry after a few milliseconds, and has more memory cells per unit area than SRAM.

ROM (slide): keeps programs and data that are permanently resident; information does not change during its life (firmware); read operation only, no write capability. The ROM part of main memory stores the bootstrap loader, which starts the computer software when power is turned on. ROM chips come in a variety of sizes.

ROM types (slide): PROM can be modified once by the user (blank PROM written once). EPROM is erased by exposing it to ultra-violet light, then rewritten. EEPROM is electrically erasable; one byte is erased at a time, so reprogramming is slow.

topics.title: Auxiliary Memory: Magnetic Tape & Magnetic Disk
notes: Auxiliary (secondary) memory is the lowest-cost, highest-capacity and slowest-access storage. It keeps programs and data for long-term storage.

Magnetic tape: plastic strip coated with magnetic material, stored on reels. Sequential access (data must be read in order). Reusable (read, write, erase). Mainly used for backup. Access time is slower than disk.

Magnetic disk: surface divided into concentric circles called tracks; tracks are divided into sectors. The minimum quantity of information that can be transferred is one sector. Disks are commonly random access (direct access).

Auxiliary memory (slide): lowest-cost, highest-capacity and slowest-access storage. It provides long-term storage for programs and data not in immediate use. Most common examples: magnetic tape and magnetic disk.
Auxiliary/secondary storage classification (slide): magnetic tape; magnetic disk (hard disk, floppy disk); optical disk (CD); flash memory (pen drive).

Magnetic tape (slide): a strip of plastic coated with a magnetic recording medium, stored on reels. Bits are recorded as magnetic spots. Sequential access storage. Reusable (read, write, erase). Usually 7 or 9 bits are recorded together with a parity bit to form a character. Only one side of the ribbon is used. Mainly used for backup. Read/write speed is slower because of sequential access.

Magnetic disk (slide): magnetized surface in spots along concentric circles called tracks. Tracks are divided into sectors; the minimum quantity of information transferred is a sector. Hard disks are permanently attached to the unit and cannot be removed by the occasional user. Read/write head moves over the surface.

topics.title: Cache Memory
notes: Cache memory is a fast and small memory placed between the CPU and main memory. It stores the active portions of the program or data.
Cache is about 10 to 100 times faster than RAM (main memory) according to the slides.

Basic operation: when the CPU needs data, the cache is checked first. If the word is found (cache hit), it is read from the fast cache. If it is not found (cache miss), main memory is accessed to read the word.
Purpose: reduce the average time to access data and improve overall system performance.
Cache (slide): a fast and small memory that stores the active portions of the program or data. It is placed between the CPU and main memory. It is 10 to 100 times faster than RAM.
Role of cache (slide): it acts as a buffer between CPU and main memory (RAM), provides faster access, and reduces the average time taken to access data, improving overall system performance.
Cache operation (slide): when the CPU needs memory, the cache is examined first. If the word is found, it is read from the fast memory. If not found, main memory is accessed to read the word.

mcq.q: Which of these is a peripheral device?
mcq.explanation: Printer is a peripheral (external) device. The others are parts of the CPU.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an impact printer?
mcq.explanation: Dot matrix is an impact printer (it strikes a ribbon). Inkjet and laser are non-impact.

mcq.q: CPU works on data in units of:
mcq.explanation: CPU works in words, peripherals work in bytes.

mcq.q: Peripheral devices are generally:
mcq.explanation: Peripherals are electro-mechanical, while the CPU is electronic.

mcq.q: Which device is a Magnetic storage device?
mcq.explanation: Hard disk stores data magnetically. The others are input or output devices.

mcq.q: MICR is used for:
options: Reading magnetic ink characters on cheques
mcq.explanation: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads cheque numbers printed in magnetic ink.

mcq.q: What is the main job of the I/O interface?
options: To transfer information between the CPU/memory and I/O devices
mcq.explanation: I/O interface transfers information between internal storage and external I/O devices.

mcq.q: Which function of the I/O interface matches the operating speed of CPU with devices?
mcq.explanation: The interface synchronizes the operating speed of CPU and I/O devices.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four interface commands?
mcq.explanation: The four commands are control, status, data output and data input.

mcq.q: In synchronous transmission, sender and receiver share:
mcq.explanation: Synchronous transmission uses a common clock to synchronize.

mcq.q: Asynchronous transmission uses which bits to mark each character?
mcq.explanation: Each character is framed by start and stop bits in asynchronous transmission.

mcq.q: Which transmission is faster?
mcq.explanation: Synchronous transmission is faster than asynchronous.

mcq.q: Which is an example of asynchronous data transfer?
mcq.explanation: Email (and forum posts) are asynchronous communication examples.

mcq.q: Handshaking signals used in source-initiated transfer are:
options: Ready for data and Data accepted
mcq.explanation: Source-initiated handshaking uses DATA VALID and DATA ACCEPTED.

mcq.q: In strobe control, the strobe signal is used to:
options: Indicate that data on the bus is valid
mcq.explanation: Strobe tells the receiver that the data is valid on the bus.

mcq.q: In Programmed I/O, who controls the data transfer?
mcq.explanation: CPU actively controls and polls the device in programmed I/O.

mcq.q: The main drawback of Programmed I/O is:
options: CPU is busy during every transfer (waste of CPU time)
mcq.explanation: CPU must check and transfer every item, wasting its time.

mcq.q: In Interrupt-initiated I/O, the interface sends a signal to the CPU when:
options: The peripheral is ready for data transfer
mcq.explanation: When the device is ready, the interface generates an interrupt.

mcq.q: Which mode transfers data directly between device and memory without CPU involvement?
mcq.explanation: DMA transfers data directly via the memory bus, freeing the CPU.

mcq.q: Which mode is most suitable for bulk transfers from a magnetic disk?
mcq.explanation: DMA is efficient for large block transfers from fast devices such as disks.

mcq.q: Primary memory is also called:
mcq.explanation: Primary memory = internal memory, directly accessible by the CPU.

mcq.q: Primary memory is:
mcq.explanation: Primary memory (RAM) is volatile: data is lost when power is off.

mcq.q: RAM stands for:
mcq.explanation: RAM = Random Access Memory.

mcq.q: Static RAM stores binary information in:
mcq.explanation: Static RAM uses flip-flops, so it needs no refreshing.

mcq.q: Dynamic RAM stores information as:
mcq.explanation: Dynamic RAM uses capacitor charge and needs periodic refresh.

mcq.q: ROM is best described as:
mcq.explanation: ROM is read-only and keeps data when power is off (non-volatile).

mcq.q: Which ROM can be erased by ultraviolet light?
mcq.explanation: EPROM is erased by exposing it to UV radiation.

mcq.q: Which ROM can be erased electrically, one byte at a time?
mcq.explanation: EEPROM is electrically erasable; one byte at a time, so it is slow to reprogram.

mcq.q: Which is the correct order of memory from fastest to slowest?
mcq.explanation: Cache is fastest, then main memory (RAM), then disk, then magnetic tape.

mcq.q: Magnetic tape provides which type of access?
mcq.explanation: Magnetic tape is a sequential access device.

mcq.q: On a magnetic disk, the concentric circles are called:
mcq.explanation: Tracks are concentric circles; tracks are divided into sectors.

mcq.q: The minimum quantity of information transferred from a magnetic disk is:
mcq.explanation: The minimum unit of transfer is a sector.

mcq.q: Magnetic tape is mainly used for:
mcq.explanation: Magnetic tape is used mostly for data backup.

mcq.q: Cache memory is placed:
mcq.explanation: Cache sits between the CPU and main memory to speed up access.

mcq.q: If the requested word is found in cache, it is called a:
mcq.explanation: Finding data in the cache is a cache hit.

short.q: What is a peripheral device? Give two examples.
short.answer: A device connected to a computer system but not part of its core architecture. Examples: monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer (any two).

short.q: Differentiate between CPU and peripheral devices (any two points).
short.answer: CPU is electronic and faster, works in words and synchronously. Peripherals are electro-mechanical, slower, work in bytes and asynchronously.

short.q: Write any two functions of an I/O interface.
short.answer: Synchronizes CPU speed with I/O device speed; selects the appropriate device; provides control and timing signals; allows data buffering (any two).

short.q: Differentiate between synchronous and asynchronous data transmission.
short.answer: Synchronous uses a common clock and fixed intervals, is faster and simpler to design. Asynchronous uses start and stop bits with irregular gaps, is slower and needs control signals (strobe or handshaking).

short.q: What is strobe control?
short.answer: A method of asynchronous transfer where a separate strobe signal tells the receiver when the data on the bus is valid.

short.q: What is handshaking? Name its two signals in source-initiated mode.
short.answer: Handshaking is a method where sender and receiver exchange control signals to confirm readiness and data acceptance. Source-initiated signals: DATA VALID and DATA ACCEPTED.

short.q: Why is handshaking more reliable than strobe control?
short.answer: In handshaking both devices confirm readiness and acceptance, so data delivery is guaranteed. Strobe only tells that data is present.

short.q: Name the three modes of data transfer between CPU and I/O.
short.answer: Programmed I/O, Interrupt-initiated I/O, Direct Memory Access (DMA).

short.q: Explain Programmed I/O briefly.
short.answer: The CPU controls every transfer by checking (polling) the device status flag and transferring data through an instruction in the program. It keeps the CPU busy and wastes time.

short.q: How does interrupt-initiated I/O improve on programmed I/O?
short.answer: The device/interface interrupts the CPU only when it is ready, so the CPU does not need to keep checking. The CPU services the transfer and then returns to its task, so less CPU time is wasted.

short.q: What is DMA and why is it used?
short.answer: Direct Memory Access lets a controller transfer data between a device and memory directly over the memory bus without CPU intervention. It is used for fast bulk transfers, such as from magnetic disks.

short.q: What are the three factors considered when selecting a memory?
short.answer: Size of memory, data access speed, and cost of memory.

short.q: Differentiate between primary and secondary memory (any two points).
short.answer: Primary: internal, directly accessible by CPU, volatile, costly, fast, smaller capacity. Secondary: external, not directly accessible, non-volatile, cheap, huge capacity, slower.

short.q: Differentiate between static RAM and dynamic RAM.
short.answer: Static RAM stores bits in flip-flops and needs no refresh; it is faster and used in cache. Dynamic RAM stores bits as charge on a capacitor and needs periodic refreshing.

short.q: What is ROM? Why is it called firmware?
short.answer: ROM is read-only non-volatile memory that stores permanent programs and data. It is called firmware because it holds information that does not change during the system's life.

short.q: Differentiate between PROM and EPROM.
short.answer: PROM can be programmed only once by the user. EPROM can be erased using UV light and reprogrammed.

short.q: Why is EEPROM reprogramming considered slow?
short.answer: EEPROM can be erased electrically but only one byte at a time, instead of erasing the whole chip in one go.

short.q: Arrange cache, main memory, magnetic disk and magnetic tape in order of access speed.
short.answer: Cache (fastest), main memory (RAM), magnetic disk, magnetic tape (slowest).

short.q: What is a magnetic tape? State its main use.
short.answer: A plastic strip coated with magnetic material on reels. It stores data sequentially and is mainly used for backup.

short.q: Explain the structure of a magnetic disk (tracks and sectors).
short.answer: A magnetic disk surface is divided into concentric circles called tracks, and each track is divided into sectors. A sector is the minimum unit of data transfer.

short.q: What is cache memory and where is it placed?
short.answer: Cache is a small, very fast memory that stores the active portions of a program or data. It is placed between the CPU and main memory.

short.q: What is a cache hit and a cache miss?
short.answer: Cache hit: the requested word is found in the cache and read quickly. Cache miss: the word is not in cache, so main memory is accessed.
